extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, and appellate practitioners (judges/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: An appellate court opinion setting and applying legal standards for patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice two-step), admissibility of expert damages opinion under FRE 702, and standards for post-trial relief on damages (Rules 59/60). It explains how those standards apply to claims to GUIs/software, CRM claims, and reasonable-royalty damages involving foreign conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step §101 analysis (directed-to/abstract-idea step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea by considering 'the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art.' Claims that focus on receipt and display of market information and use of that information to place orders are directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court analyzes the claimed advance (not merely individual claim elements) and compares to precedent (e.g., Enfish, IBG II/III). A claimed combination of receipt and display of information, even in a particular arrangement, can be an abstract idea if it amounts to 'graphing bids and offers to assist a trader to make an order.' Focus on whether the claim improves computer functionality or merely uses generic computers to automate manual processes (the latter is abstract).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice step two — inventive-concept requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to an abstract idea, determine whether the claim adds 'something significantly more'—an inventive concept—beyond the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract idea itself cannot supply the inventive concept. Courts look at claim elements 'individually and as an ordered combination.' Mere conventional activities (e.g., receiving market information, displaying indicators along a price axis, use of preexisting computers/displays) do not supply an inventive concept. An improvement must be to computer functionality (not merely better presentation of information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate claims by their asserted limitations (claims measure the invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim element is material to defining the scope of the patent; infringement and eligibility are assessed with respect to each asserted claim as a separate entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee's rights extend only to the claimed combination of elements. Courts construe claims (including prosecution history) to determine scope (e.g., how 'static price axis' is construed can alter the analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement acts under 35 U.S.C. §271(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct infringement under §271(a) consists of making, using, offering to sell, selling, or importing the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For method claims, direct infringement occurs only by practicing the method. For CRM (computer-readable medium) claims, infringement requires making (or other §271 act) of tangible copies/CRMs. A damages theory must start from an act of infringement as defined by the asserted claims; a theory that rests on 'making' in the abstract or on the software itself without tying to making a claimed CRM or performing the method is legally insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software vs. tangible copy distinction (Microsoft precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Software 'in the abstract' is distinct from a particular tangible 'copy' on a computer-readable medium; software itself may not qualify as a 'component' under §271(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expert theory that treats 'BookTrader' as an abstract made product (detached from any medium) fails to address the claimed CRM or method; damages must link to infringing acts of the claimed subject matter (e.g., copies/CRMs sold or made).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of expert testimony under FRE 702 requires a correct legal premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert damages testimony is excludable under Rule 702 if it is 'premised on a misapplication of controlling law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A damages theory that includes foreign damages without a legally sound basis (e.g., relying on foreseeability alone contrary to controlling precedent) can be excluded. Courts must ensure experts' opinions rest on correct legal standards (e.g., proper proximate-cause principles, statutory reach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on extraterritorial recovery — Power Integrations principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally U.S. patent law 'does not operate extraterritorially' and a patentee may not recover damages for worldwide sales merely because those foreign sales were the foreseeable result of domestic infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After establishing domestic infringement acts, recovery for foreign exploitation requires more than foreseeability; courts rely on proximate-cause analysis and statutory context to determine whether foreign sales can be included in damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: WesternGeco and proximate-cause framework for foreign damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate (as in WesternGeco for §271(f)(2)), foreign lost profits proximately caused by domestic infringement may be recoverable, but recovery requires showing a causal relationship between the domestic infringement (the infringement) and the foreign conduct for which recovery is sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WesternGeco's holding focused on lost profits under §271(f)(2); its implications for reasonable-royalty damages or §271(a) claims are not automatic. Courts must apply proximate-cause requirements and consider the statutory nature of the claim when assessing inclusion of foreign damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximate cause — foreseeability alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination whether foreign conduct may be included in damages requires proximate-cause analysis — foreseeability alone does not establish proximate cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'reasonable, objective foreseeability' standard applied in lost-profits cases (e.g., Rite-Hite) may not directly translate to reasonable-royalty damages; courts must analyze whether the statutory cause of action permits the extraterritorial link via proximate causation and consider consequences of expanding reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible bases to include foreign users in royalty calculations (evidentiary link to domestic acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign users may be included in damages if there is evidence linking their copies/uses to domestic acts that can constitute infringement—examples: making a copy via a U.S. server; sale in the United States via a Customer Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District court allowed damages evidence based on copying via domestic servers and domestic sales through customer agreements, but disallowed inclusion premised merely on domestic 'making' of the accused product with worldwide damages absent the required causal/infringement link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment requirement in reasonable-royalty damages
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty must be apportioned to reflect the value attributable to the claimed invention; royalties cannot include value for unclaimed upgrades or features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether to include foreign-made copies or later-upgraded CRMs in royalty bases, courts consider whether incremental value is attributable to the claimed invention; experts must provide a concrete apportionment tied to claimed elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and the hypothetical negotiation date
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable-royalty analysis is anchored to a hypothetical negotiation at a specified date (here, the date a patent issued) and should reflect the parties' bargaining positions and relevant facts at that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value from pre-issue development that was non-infringing cannot be retroactively converted into royaltyable domestic infringement; experts must align their royalty bases with facts as of the hypothetical negotiation and avoid including value from pre-existing non-infringing exploitation unless legally justified and apportioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 702 exclusion reinforces requirement to tie damages theory to infringement as claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert theories that do not focus on the infringement defined by the asserted claims (e.g., failing to start from making a claimed CRM or practicing the claimed method) are legally insufficient and subject to exclusion under Rule 702.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not 'rewrite' an expert's theory to make it conform to the claims; experts and counsel must structure their damages theories to begin from infringing acts that the law recognizes for the asserted claim types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for new trial or relief under Rules 59 and 60(b)(3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief for discovery abuse, withheld information, or fraud at trial is extraordinary and requires a showing that justifies granting a new trial or setting aside judgment (e.g., withheld evidence, false testimony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply an 'abuse of discretion' standard on appeal. Motions under Rule 60(b)(3) are 'extraordinary' and cannot be used to present evidence that with due diligence could have been introduced before judgment; parties have a duty to investigate facts before trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM-review determinations do not dictate §101 eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior determination that patents are not eligible for CBM review (or vice versa) does not determine the merits of a §101 eligibility analysis in district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inquiries under CBM and §101 are related but distinct; a CBM qualification ruling does not bind or foreclose a later §101 eligibility decision on the merits.
